page.h1: Messaging for on-demand and field services
page.metaTitle: Messaging for on-demand and field services
page.metaDescription: Job dispatch, arrival windows and technician ETA messages over the messaging accounts your operation already holds.
page.lede: Field service messaging is measured in minutes: a technician twenty minutes away, a job that moved, a customer who will not be in. Send the ETA when the event happens and it saves a trip; send it late and it is worse than silence.

sections.h: The messages that protect the day’s schedule
bullets: Technician en-route notice with an ETA

sections.h: Send-time is the constraint, not volume
p: An ETA message that arrives late is worse than no message. Because provider limits apply per sender number, a wide dispatch at the same minute can queue behind itself — which is exactly why pacing is configured per number and visible in the console rather than hidden behind one shared allowance.
bullets: Per-number pacing so a dispatch burst drains predictably
Sender selection so operational traffic uses the right number
Automatic failover between connected SMS accounts

sections.h: It fits alongside your dispatch system
p: Dispatch stays with your dispatch system, which knows the technician’s route and the customer’s address. The platform sends the message it is told to send and reports whether it left — so the two systems keep the jobs they are good at.

faq.q: Can we send from a different number for each region?
faq.a: You connect the numbers you own and choose which one a send uses, so a per-region number is a configuration rather than a code change.

faq.q: Will the platform hold messages and send them later?
faq.a: Scheduled and bulk sending exist as console features. They do not turn the platform into a task queue for time-critical traffic; for ETAs, send when the event happens.

faq.q: How do we know a dispatch notice went out?
faq.a: Each send is logged with its status, and delivery receipts can be pushed to your own endpoint. A receipt confirms the destination network accepted the message, not that the customer read it.
